evidence.quote:
the death of his only son so unsettled him that he immediately
left England, accompanied by two companions, his old fellow-voyagers,
Sir Henry Curtis and Captain Good, and has now utterly vanished into the
dark heart of Africa
evidence.paraphrase: Quatermain, unsettled by his son's death, departs England and disappears into Africa.

evidence.quote:
One letter only have I received from the old gentleman, dated from a
mission station high up the Tana, a river on the east coast, about three
hundred miles north of Zanzibar.
evidence.paraphrase: The narrator locates Quatermain's last communication at a remote African river far from Zanzibar.

evidence.quote:
I remember that I hesitated a little
before going in, there was such an air of desolation about the spot.
evidence.paraphrase: The narrator hesitates upon sensing the desolation of the deserted kraal.

evidence.quote:
she
told me that all the people whom I had seen had died of fever. When
they had died the other inhabitants of the kraal had taken the cattle
and gone away, leaving the poor old woman
evidence.paraphrase: A fever epidemic killed the kraal's inhabitants, and survivors abandoned an old woman.

evidence.quote:
Those people carry the doctrine of the survival of
the fittest to its extreme, you see.
evidence.paraphrase: The narrator frames the abandonment of the old woman as an extreme application of survival of the fittest.

evidence.quote:
I took the smoothbore because it shot a bullet very well; and my experience has
been that a round ball from a smoothbore is quite as effective against a
lion as an express bullet. The lion is soft, and not a difficult animal
to finish if you hit him anywhere in the body.
evidence.paraphrase: The narrator explains the technical reasoning behind his choice of weapon and how to kill a lion.

evidence.quote:
the first thing I set to work to do was to try to
discover whereabouts the brutes lay up for the day.
evidence.paraphrase: The narrator sets out to investigate where the lions rested during the day.

evidence.quote:
Before I had got half-way
round the pan I found the remains of a blue vilderbeeste that had
evidently been killed within the last three or four days and partially
devoured by lions; and from other indications about I was soon assured
that if the family were not in the pan that day they spent a good deal
of their spare time there.
evidence.paraphrase: The narrator reasons from physical evidence to conclude the lions frequented the pan.

evidence.quote:
this first gave me the
idea of firing the reeds, which, as I think I told you, were pretty dry.
evidence.paraphrase: The narrator devises a plan to use the wind to set fire to the reeds to flush out the lions.

evidence.quote:
there I lay shaking
with terror, and the cold perspiration pouring out of me
evidence.paraphrase: The narrator describes lying paralyzed with terror as the lions fed nearby.

evidence.quote:
the next those great white
teeth of his had met in my thigh--I heard them grate against the bone. I
yelled out in agony
evidence.paraphrase: The lion seizes the narrator's thigh in its teeth, causing agonizing injury.

evidence.quote:
I have been lame ever
since, and shall be to my dying day; in the month of March the wound
always troubles me a great deal, and every three years it breaks out
raw.
evidence.paraphrase: The lion attack left the narrator permanently lame with a recurring wound.
